records.heading: Introduction
records.content:
# Book 01 — Business Fundamentals, Economics & Competitive Strategy

Edition: October 2026. Research cutoff: October 19, 2026.

records.heading: 1. Start with the business mechanism
records.content:
A growth strategy explains how a business can create more valuable customer relationships while remaining able to deliver its promises. It connects customer demand, an attractive offer, distribution, operations, and cash. A marketing activity belongs in that strategy only when the team can describe which connection it strengthens. Publishing more material may increase attention without improving demand. Buying more traffic may expose a broken onboarding process. Selling more annual subscriptions may improve this month's cash while creating a service obligation that lasts a year.

The first discipline is therefore to write the business mechanism in ordinary language. Who experiences a costly problem? What do they do today? Who can authorize a purchase? What changes after buying? How does the business receive money? What must it spend to deliver the result? What brings the customer back? These questions work for software, professional services, commerce, local services, and businesses selling through distributors. Their answers differ, so the same marketing recommendation cannot be transferred indiscriminately between them.

Consider a hypothetical bookkeeping service. Its problem might be late financial reporting for small employers. The buyer may be the owner, while an office manager supplies documents. Revenue arrives monthly, but onboarding requires concentrated labor. More leads are useful only if qualified prospects understand the reporting promise and the team has capacity to onboard them. A plan that maximizes booked calls while ignoring onboarding hours can increase apparent demand and reduce service quality simultaneously.

In ClimbOS, capture this mechanism as a dated business snapshot before selecting channels. Represent uncertainty explicitly: an unknown buying role is a research task, not permission to invent one. Store owner statements separately from integration measurements. The snapshot should make it possible to reconstruct why a recommendation was sensible at the time, even after prices, product capabilities, or market conditions change.

This book develops an original decision method for that work. The calculations and examples are educational scenarios, not industry benchmarks or reported results. Its strategic foundations include Porter's emphasis on distinctive activities, fit, and trade-offs, rather than merely performing familiar activities more efficiently. [Harvard Institute for Strategy and Competitiveness](https://www.isc.hbs.edu/strategy/creating-a-successful-strategy/Pages/default.aspx).

records.heading: 2. Separate goals, diagnosis, strategy, and tactics
records.content:
A goal names an outcome. A diagnosis explains the constraint preventing it. A strategy chooses a coherent way to address that constraint. Tactics are the individual actions that implement the choice. Confusing these levels produces plans that sound active but cannot guide difficult decisions. “Grow revenue” is a goal; “post daily” is a tactic; neither explains why a customer should buy or why that action deserves scarce resources.

Write a diagnosis as a falsifiable causal statement: “Qualified buyers abandon evaluation because implementation effort appears greater than the expected benefit.” Then list the evidence and competing explanations. Perhaps prospects are simply outside the target segment. Perhaps the product lacks a critical capability. Perhaps prices are unclear. The diagnosis remains provisional until evidence distinguishes these possibilities. A useful strategy might reduce implementation uncertainty through a narrow onboarding offer, demonstrable setup steps, and explicit qualification.

Use a four-part strategy memo. First, state the customer and situation being prioritized. Second, identify the obstacle with its evidence. Third, describe the chosen approach and the activities it requires. Fourth, state what will be deferred. The last part matters because a strategy that accepts every opportunity does not resolve resource conflicts. An inexpensive self-service offer and a deeply customized enterprise service can both be attractive businesses, but combining them without separate economics can make each perform poorly.

A practical decision tree begins with evidence of a real problem. If evidence is weak, research comes before scaling acquisition. If demand exists but customers do not activate, improve the path to value. If activation works but retention is weak, investigate recurring usefulness and service quality. If retained customers are profitable and delivery capacity exists, test more distribution. If the business cannot finance the delay between spending and collection, fix financing or payment terms before increasing acquisition commitments.

ClimbOS should render these branches as a recommendation with supporting observations, alternative explanations, and a next discriminating test. Avoid a single opaque “growth score.” Two businesses can receive the same score while needing opposite actions. A structured diagnosis preserves the causal reasoning the owner needs to challenge. Its acceptance criterion is that another reviewer can explain what finding would make the recommendation change.

records.heading: 3. Model the business without mistaking the map for evidence
records.content:
The Business Model Canvas offers a compact way to relate customers, value, delivery, resources, revenue, and costs. Strategyzer presents it as a model of how a business creates, delivers, and captures value, with nine connected blocks. The canvas is a useful organizing reference; a completed canvas does not establish that the underlying assumptions are true. [Official Business Model Canvas](https://www.strategyzer.com/library/the-business-model-canvas).

For practical use, attach an evidence state to each important connection. A customer segment might be supported by invoices, interviews, or only the founder's belief. A distribution channel might exist technically but never have produced a retained customer. A partnership might be signed but inactive. This makes the model operational: the most consequential weak connection becomes a candidate for validation. The objective is not to fill every box with confident prose. It is to identify which unsupported belief could make the business fail.

Take a hypothetical Mac application sold with a perpetual license. The customer receives local utility and may expect compatibility updates. Revenue arrives once, while support and maintenance continue. A subscription model for the same application changes the promise: customers may now judge whether continuing value justifies recurring payment. Neither arrangement is automatically superior. The team must investigate purchase preferences, service obligations, refund behavior, update costs, and the cost of reaching customers under each model.

Compare alternatives using consistent accounting periods. A perpetual license receiving $48 today cannot be compared directly with a $6 monthly subscription using only the first month. Build cash and contribution schedules over a stated horizon. Include the possibility of refunds, cancellations, upgrades, and support. Keep uncertain future upgrades out of the base case until evidence supports them. The result may favor a simpler model despite a less exciting revenue headline.

ClimbOS can store competing business models as scenario objects referencing the same customer evidence. The interface should highlight the assumptions that differ, rather than generating two unrelated essays. A model comparison becomes actionable when it names a low-cost test: a pricing interview, an optional maintenance package, a clearly disclosed pilot, or a landing-page comprehension study. Do not change a real customer's contractual terms merely to run an experiment.

records.heading: 4. Understand the unit before calculating unit economics
records.content:
A unit is the object whose revenue and cost relationship you want to understand. It might be an order, account, seat, project, appointment, location, or fulfilled subscription month. Choosing the wrong unit can hide losses. A profitable order does not imply a profitable customer if returns are expensive. A profitable seat does not imply a profitable account when a large customer requires extensive custom support. A profitable project does not imply a profitable agency if unpaid proposals consume the team's time.

Define a unit contract with the unit name, observation period, currency, revenue recognition basis, included costs, and exclusions. Then calculate contribution as revenue attributable to that unit minus the costs that change because the unit exists or is served. Use gross margin and contribution margin consistently but do not assume they mean the same thing across organizations. The business must state its own accounting boundaries and reconcile management metrics with its accounting system.

A hypothetical ecommerce order produces $90 after discounts and expected refunds. Product and packaging cost $37, payment processing costs $3, and fulfillment costs $10. Contribution before acquisition is $40. If incremental acquisition cost is $26, contribution after acquisition is $14. That is different from saying the company has a $14 profit: rent, management, software, and other fixed expenses still need coverage. If the campaign shifts existing customers into paid clicks, the incremental economics may be worse than the attributed economics suggest.

For an AI software product, useful variable costs may include model calls, research services, generated media, email sends, storage operations, and support effort attributable to usage. Not every infrastructure cost is perfectly variable. Allocate shared expenses transparently and show sensitivity when the allocation changes the decision. A heavy user costing far more than the average can make a plan unprofitable even if the average account looks healthy.

ClimbOS should calculate financial results deterministically from typed inputs. A model may explain the formula, but it should not silently choose cost categories, exchange rates, or billing periods. Require explicit confirmation of a unit definition before showing comparisons. Return “insufficient inputs” when key costs are unknown, while offering a scenario range that clearly labels those missing costs as assumptions.

records.heading: 5. Contribution, margin targets, and break-even
records.content:
The basic formulas are straightforward:

- Contribution = net revenue − defined variable costs.
- Contribution margin = contribution / net revenue, when net revenue is positive.
- Break-even units = fixed costs / contribution per unit, when unit contribution is positive; round up when units must be whole.
- Price required for target margin = variable cost / (1 − target margin), under the stated cost model.

The last formula is frequently confused with markup. Adding 30% to a cost of $10 produces a $13 price and a margin of about 23.1%. Achieving a 30% margin requires a price of approximately $14.29. This difference matters when ClimbOS evaluates plans intended to maintain at least a 30% margin. The requirement must specify whether it covers only usage costs, all service delivery costs, or a wider allocation including support and infrastructure.

Suppose a hypothetical ClimbOS plan has $12 in expected monthly model and research expense, $2 in email and infrastructure allocation, and $4 in variable support. The defined service cost is $18. A price of $25 yields $7 contribution, or 28%. A $30 price yields $12, or 40%. These figures are scenarios, not current vendor prices or a recommended public price. They omit taxes, payment fees, refunds, acquisition, and fixed costs unless those are separately added to the model.

Break-even adds another perspective. If monthly fixed expenses are hypothetically $6,000 and each account contributes $12 after the defined service costs, 500 active paying accounts cover those expenses before other omitted items. But this steady-state result says nothing about how long acquisition takes or how much cash funds growth. A business can have attractive steady-state economics and still run out of cash while building its customer base.

Use margin scenarios across usage levels rather than a single average. At minimum, evaluate light, typical, and heavy usage with explicit assumptions. Consider concurrency and retry storms as well as individual request cost. If a plan's promised usage can exceed its sustainable cost envelope, adjust packaging, include fair metering, or change the execution policy before launch. Hiding expensive work behind an unlimited label does not remove its economic consequences.

records.heading: 6. Acquisition costs and the danger of convenient denominators
records.content:
Customer acquisition cost requires both a cost boundary and a customer boundary. Paid media CAC might include only ad spend. Fully loaded CAC might include relevant labor, agencies, creative, sales tooling, and commissions. Both can be useful, but they answer different questions. A channel comparison using ad-only cost for one channel and fully loaded cost for another creates a misleading ranking.

Define the denominator carefully. A signup is not a paying customer. A paying customer who immediately refunds may not qualify as a successful acquisition under the decision being evaluated. For a recurring business, report acquisition cohorts and their subsequent retention. For sales-led businesses, account for the time between lead generation, sales effort, signed agreement, and collected payment. A monthly snapshot may pair today's spend with customers generated by earlier spending.

A hypothetical campaign spends $600 and produces 100 signups, 20 activated accounts, and 5 paying accounts within the declared conversion window. Cost per signup is $6, cost per activation is $30, and ad-only CAC is $120. If sales and creative work add $400, fully loaded acquisition cost for those five customers is $200 each. Neither number establishes incrementality: some customers may have arrived without the campaign. Report the distinction rather than choosing the more flattering metric.

Payback measures how long customer contribution takes to recover acquisition expense. With a stable monthly contribution of $25, a $200 acquisition cost implies eight months under a simplified model. Real cohorts may cancel, expand, receive refunds, or incur higher onboarding costs. A more useful calculation accumulates expected contribution month by month until it covers acquisition. If the cumulative amount never covers it within the modeled horizon, report that explicitly.

ClimbOS should display the denominator beside every cost metric. A card labeled “$30 CAC” must not actually mean cost per activated signup. Preserve channel attribution rules and conversion windows as metadata. When data is too sparse, show counts and intervals or a scenario instead of presenting precision that the underlying evidence cannot support.

records.heading: 7. Lifetime value without fictional lifetimes
records.content:
Lifetime value can be a useful planning concept, but it becomes dangerous when a short observation window is extrapolated into years of certain revenue. Begin with observed contribution over a fixed horizon. Then add an explicit forecast for the unobserved period. Keep those components separate. The owner should see how much of the claimed value is earned and how much depends on assumptions about retention, expansion, prices, or cost.

A cohort-based contribution model can be written as the sum, across future periods, of probability of remaining active multiplied by expected net revenue less expected servicing cost, optionally discounted. Account for different customer segments when behavior differs materially. A simple revenue-divided-by-churn shortcut assumes conditions that may not fit a growing, seasonal, or heterogeneous business. Treat it as a limited approximation, not a law.

Imagine a hypothetical cohort of 100 customers. Across three months, collected revenue is $8,000 and defined service cost is $2,600. Observed contribution is $5,400, or $54 per initial customer. A proposed six-month forecast adds another $30 per initial customer under a retention scenario. Report observed three-month contribution of $54 and forecast additional contribution of $30; do not label the entire $84 as measured lifetime value. If acquisition cost was $65, the observed cohort has not yet paid back.

Use scenario analysis to expose the important uncertainty. Vary retention, expansion, and serving cost independently where plausible. Avoid changing every assumption optimistically at once. If a channel is attractive only under the highest retention case, the next useful task is often to validate retention, not to increase channel spend. The business may also choose a short cash payback requirement even when modeled long-run value is attractive.

In ClimbOS, store observed and forecast contribution in different fields, with cohort definitions and time horizons. Never allow a generated paragraph to erase that distinction. Link every assumption to its owner, rationale, sensitivity, and review date. Book 12 extends the statistical and forecasting methods; the strategic rule here is that uncertainty should change investment size and evidence collection, not disappear inside a ratio.

records.heading: 8. Cash, capacity, and the growth ceiling
records.content:
Cash collection and economic value are related but different. An annual prepayment provides cash now while creating future delivery obligations. A large service contract may recognize revenue while payment arrives later. Inventory may be paid for before customers buy it. Growth increases these timing differences. A business should model a cash schedule alongside contribution so that a profitable plan does not exceed available financing.

Construct a rolling schedule with starting cash, expected collections, committed outflows, discretionary investment, and ending cash. Label uncertain collections rather than treating pipeline as money in the bank. Stress-test delayed payments, refunds, lower conversion, and unexpectedly expensive delivery. A useful investment gate asks whether the business remains above its chosen minimum cash buffer in a plausible downside case. That buffer is an owner policy, not a universal percentage.

Capacity is equally concrete. A service company with 80 available delivery hours cannot responsibly sell 120 hours merely because lead generation is inexpensive. A software team may face support or onboarding bottlenecks even when digital delivery scales. A local provider has geography and scheduling constraints. Model the limiting resource in the same units as demand: consultations, installation slots, shipping capacity, support hours, or concurrent processing jobs.

A hypothetical agency can onboard two new projects per month without harming existing work. A campaign forecasting six project wins is not ready to scale unless the team plans additional capacity or staggers starts. The appropriate marketing strategy may emphasize higher-fit projects, deposits, waitlists, referral partners, or improved qualification. Increasing lead volume could be the least valuable intervention.

ClimbOS should make capacity a first-class constraint in channel planning. Ask owners for a comfortable operating range, then compare proposed demand with that range. When capacity is unknown, show the operational question that must be answered. An AI assistant can summarize bookings and support loads, but the business should approve assumptions about hiring, quality standards, or acceptable customer waiting time.

records.heading: 9. Competitive advantage is a system of choices
records.content:
A differentiator matters only if customers value it, the business can deliver it, and competitors cannot erase its usefulness immediately at acceptable cost. “AI-powered,” “premium,” and “easy to use” are descriptions, not demonstrated advantages. Test the customer consequence: what task becomes easier, what risk falls, what decision becomes possible, or what result arrives sooner? Then examine whether the supporting activities reinforce one another.

Porter's trade-off framework explains why pursuing incompatible positions can undermine strategic coherence. The practical lesson is to connect an attractive promise to operating choices and explicit limits. [Harvard explanation of strategic trade-offs](https://www.isc.hbs.edu/strategy/creating-a-successful-strategy/Pages/making-strategic-trade-offs.aspx). The analysis below applies that idea to original hypothetical situations; it does not reproduce a company case study.

For a software utility focused on privacy-sensitive professionals, an advantage hypothesis might combine local processing, clear data controls, dependable offline behavior, and support documentation that explains those properties. Marketing alone cannot create the position. The product architecture, defaults, pricing, onboarding, and support must support it. If the team later makes remote processing mandatory for a key task, it should revisit the strategic promise rather than quietly retaining the old message.

A low-price position needs its own reinforcing system: limited customization, controlled support expense, efficient self-service, clear scope, and a sustainable distribution model. Offering unlimited bespoke assistance while competing on the lowest price may be a deliberate acquisition investment, but it should not be mistaken for a sustainable model until the economics support it. Strategic coherence requires the team to admit where a good opportunity belongs to a different business model.

Build an advantage review with four tests: customer relevance, delivery evidence, economic compatibility, and durability. Score each with a written rationale, not merely a number. Ask how a competitor could respond and what assets accumulate through repeated delivery. ClimbOS should propose advantage hypotheses and evidence gaps; it should not declare a moat from a homepage claim. Evidence of repeated customer preference is stronger than the founder's choice of adjectives.

records.heading: 10. Segment before prioritizing
records.content:
Segmentation is commercially useful when different groups need different choices. Demographic labels alone may not change the strategy. More useful dimensions include urgency, buying trigger, workflow complexity, implementation burden, risk, available budget, purchase authority, and route to reach the buyer. The same-sized companies may require entirely different sales and product approaches because one has an urgent compliance deadline and another is casually exploring improvements.

Start with a segment definition that a team member can apply consistently. Specify inclusion and exclusion rules, observable signals, the relevant buying situation, and a path to verify those signals. Avoid a segment like “all businesses that want to grow.” A narrower hypothetical segment could be independent service firms with recurring client work, an owner managing sales, and difficulty following up on inbound inquiries. That definition suggests research questions without claiming the segment is already proven.

Evaluate segments using a gate followed by a comparison. The gate rejects segments the business cannot serve lawfully, competently, or economically. The comparison considers problem severity, willingness and ability to pay, reachability, time to value, retention potential, competition, and strategic fit. Weights are explicit decision policies. They do not transform weak evidence into objective truth. Record confidence for each rating and test whether reasonable changes in weights alter the preferred segment.

A small high-fit segment can be a better starting market than a large poorly reachable one. Initial focus allows the team to learn a repeated buying process and build reusable proof. Expansion becomes more credible when the team can state what transfers to the adjacent segment and what must change. An agency moving from local clinics to ecommerce brands may retain design capabilities while changing buyers, sales cycles, compliance considerations, and proof requirements.

ClimbOS should maintain segment-specific assumptions, economics, and evidence. Do not average all accounts into a single ideal customer profile when their costs and retention differ. Let the owner compare the priority segment with a runner-up, including the strongest reason the runner-up could win. This encourages reasoned choice rather than a polished recommendation that conceals alternatives.

records.heading: 11. Manage the offer and portfolio
records.content:
An offer combines an outcome, scope, delivery method, conditions, price, and risk allocation. Two products with similar features can have different offers because one includes implementation, a limited pilot, a migration service, or a clear usage allowance. Before building another feature, investigate whether buyers understand what they receive and what effort they must contribute. Confusion can resemble lack of demand.

Offer design should remove uncertainty honestly. Specify who the offer suits, what is included, what is excluded, how long delivery takes under stated conditions, and what happens when requirements change. Guarantees require operational and financial support. Avoid promises about revenue growth that the provider cannot control. A narrower process guarantee may be feasible where an outcome guarantee is not, but even that needs explicit terms and a clear fulfillment mechanism.

Portfolio decisions compare the opportunity cost of supporting multiple offers. Each additional product or plan creates acquisition, onboarding, documentation, maintenance, and support work. A founder with several applications may gain shared distribution and brand recognition, yet still fragment attention. Calculate which assets truly transfer and which merely share a logo. A common checkout is useful; an unfocused roadmap can still weaken every product.

Use an investment ledger with maintain, improve, test, and retire decisions. Maintain means the product receives enough attention to meet its promises. Improve means a specific constraint merits focused work. Test means an uncertain opportunity receives a bounded experiment. Retire requires a customer transition plan and fulfillment of obligations. Do not let a score automatically remove access or change subscriptions. Portfolio governance affects real customers.

ClimbOS can assist by comparing contribution, demand evidence, delivery burden, and strategic learning across offers. Separate current revenue from future potential, and distinguish customer commitments from discretionary roadmap work. Recommend a manageable number of concurrent growth projects based on actual capacity. The aim is concentrated learning and reliable delivery, not the appearance of a large opportunity pipeline.

records.heading: 12. Sequence investment under uncertainty
records.content:
A growth budget is a portfolio of commitments with different reversibility and learning value. Interviews, prototypes, limited campaigns, annual software contracts, permanent hires, and inventory purchases do not create the same obligations. Invest in evidence before making the commitments that depend on it. This is especially important when the team's confidence comes from enthusiastic feedback rather than observed buying behavior.

A useful sequence moves from problem evidence to offer comprehension, purchase intent, paid adoption, repeat value, and scalable acquisition. The sequence is not perfectly linear. Existing businesses may already have strong evidence in some areas, and sales-led products may need a paid pilot to test several assumptions together. The discipline is to state which assumption the next investment addresses and what result would justify a larger commitment.

Evaluate an experiment using decision value rather than only expected revenue. A small test that rules out an expensive mistake can be valuable even when it produces no customers. Conversely, a campaign producing a handful of customers may teach little if targeting, messaging, and conversion tracking are all changed simultaneously. Design the test so that its outcome informs a specific decision.

For a hypothetical $600 monthly advertising ceiling, do not automatically spend the full amount. If landing-page analytics are unreliable, reserve spending while validating the measurement path. If the product cannot accept payments, use the time to resolve that issue. If a small test reveals a credible acquisition route, retain enough budget to confirm the result rather than scattering money across every platform. A ceiling protects resources; it is not a utilization target.

ClimbOS should label commitments by reversibility, cash timing, and evidence requirements. Forecasts should show ranges and the assumptions driving them. The owner can then decide whether to pay for speed, reduce scope, or collect more evidence. An automated plan should never confuse a positive expected value estimate with certainty that the business can tolerate the downside.

records.heading: 13. AI-native opportunities in strategic work
records.content:
AI can reduce the cost of assembling evidence, comparing alternatives, drafting experiments, and maintaining decision records. Its strongest strategic role is often to make reasoning inspectable and repeated work consistent. It can extract stated prices from approved pages, classify interview excerpts, compare cost scenarios, and identify contradictions between a promised service level and observed capacity. These outputs still need reliable inputs and evaluation.

Separate four activities: extraction, analysis, proposal, and execution. Extraction records what a source says. Analysis explains implications under assumptions. Proposal recommends a choice. Execution changes something outside the analysis environment. Combining all four into one unreviewed response makes it difficult to detect where an error entered. A structured workflow lets ClimbOS validate facts and arithmetic before asking an owner to approve a concrete plan.

For customer research, a model can group interview observations by buying trigger and obstacle, but should preserve the original excerpts and dissenting cases. For economics, it can identify missing inputs and explain a deterministic calculation, but should not invent service costs. For strategy, it can generate competing approaches with trade-offs, but should not treat persuasive language as evidence. For monitoring, it can flag changed conditions that require a new decision rather than automatically rewriting the strategy every day.

Automation becomes more useful when the action boundary is narrow. A weekly internal diagnostic can run with read-only analytics and a bounded compute budget. A pricing change, outbound campaign, or increase in advertising spend requires a different permission scope. Existing owner authorization can cover routine actions within explicit limits, but access to an integration alone does not define those limits. Design permissions around business consequences.

In ClimbOS, store the model version, evidence snapshot, prompt version, calculation version, and reviewer decision for important recommendations. Evaluate whether the assistant finds material constraints, distinguishes facts from hypotheses, and changes its advice when inputs change. The success criterion is better decisions with less owner effort, not a larger number of generated reports.

records.heading: 14. A complete hypothetical business diagnostic
records.content:
Consider an invented subscription product called Northstar Desk. It serves small service teams, charges $40 monthly, and has 80 paying accounts. These are scenario inputs, not verified facts about any real product. The owner wants 20 additional paying accounts in 90 days, can spend at most $600 monthly on ads, and has ten hours weekly for growth work. Defined monthly service costs average $12 per account, with higher support expense during onboarding.

First, calculate the current contribution before acquisition and fixed expenses: 80 × ($40 − $12) = $2,240 monthly. That does not establish company profit. Next, inspect retention and acquisition evidence. Suppose only three months of cohort data exist and some cancellation reasons are missing. Lifetime value is therefore uncertain. Do not justify an aggressive acquisition program using a mature steady-state retention assumption the business has never observed.

Second, diagnose the funnel. Suppose the owner provides records showing that many qualified trials reach setup but do not complete the first useful workflow. Interviews indicate that configuration terminology is confusing. This is evidence for an activation obstacle, but other explanations remain possible: users may lack the underlying data or may have selected the wrong product. Design an onboarding comparison with observed task completion and brief follow-up interviews. Avoid claiming the interface change caused revenue improvement before measuring downstream behavior.

Third, compare strategies. Strategy A increases paid trial volume immediately. Strategy B improves first-value completion and uses existing interested leads for a permissioned re-engagement test. Strategy C sells a high-touch onboarding package. Compare each against cash, support capacity, user preference, and learning value. If the owner cannot deliver the service in C and activation weakness makes A wasteful, B may be the best first experiment. This is a conditional recommendation, not a universal rule.

Finally, define the review. Measure eligible trial count, first-value completion within the stated window, paid conversion, support minutes, refunds, and cohort contribution. Record every numerator and denominator. If task completion improves but paid conversion does not, investigate value and buyer fit instead of declaring success. ClimbOS should preserve this chain from evidence through choice and outcome so future recommendations learn from the actual result.

records.heading: 15. Machine-readable diagnostic and investment playbooks
records.content:
The following contracts are proposed knowledge artifacts. They are valid YAML and JSON examples, not installed integrations. The numerical limits in them are illustrative owner policies. Production adapters must validate identifiers, permissions, cost reservations, and current business constraints before acting.

```yaml
id: b01-business-diagnostic
version: 1
mode: analysis_only
required_inputs:
  - business_snapshot_id
  - goal_definition
  - currency
  - observation_window
  - cost_boundary
  - capacity_definition
steps:
  - id: identity
    instruction: Verify canonical business and separate reported from measured facts.
  - id: mechanism
    instruction: Map buyer, problem, offer, delivery, collection, and repeat value.
  - id: economics
    instruction: Calculate contribution using explicit cost inclusions and exclusions.
  - id: diagnosis
    instruction: Compare demand, activation, retention, capacity, and cash constraints.
  - id: alternatives
    instruction: Produce competing approaches with evidence and trade-offs.
  - id: decision
    instruction: Select a bounded experiment or request material missing evidence.
outputs:
  - diagnosis_with_counterevidence
  - unit_economics_with_assumptions
  - alternatives_and_deferred_work
  - experiment_and_review_date
stop_conditions:
  - unresolved_business_identity
  - inconsistent_currency_or_period
  - missing_authorization_for_external_action
```

```json
{
  "id": "b01-investment-gate",
  "version": 1,
  "status": "proposed_policy",
  "requirements": {
    "positive_unit_contribution": true,
    "cash_downside_reviewed": true,
    "delivery_capacity_reviewed": true,
    "measurement_definition_present": true,
    "explicit_budget_authorization": true
  },
  "outcomes": ["eligible_for_owner_review", "collect_evidence", "reject_with_reason"],
  "missing_input_behavior": "return_unknown_and_name_the_missing_input",
  "execution_permission": "none"
}
```

Use the diagnostic when a business first joins ClimbOS, after a material product change, or when outcomes contradict the current strategy. Do not rerun every component merely because a schedule exists. Refresh the affected assumptions and preserve the previous version. Use the investment gate before scaling a commercial offer; a failing gate should identify a repairable condition rather than produce an unexplained refusal. A deliberately loss-making learning experiment needs a separate, explicit loss ceiling and owner-approved learning objective; it must not be mislabeled as passing the positive-contribution scaling gate.

records.heading: 16. Implement the knowledge in ClimbOS
records.content:
A practical implementation needs business snapshots, segments, offers, evidence claims, unit definitions, cost schedules, capacity records, decisions, experiments, and outcomes. Each record belongs to a tenant and references the relevant version. Avoid storing important economics only inside narrative reports. Structured records allow recalculation when a price or cost changes and help distinguish a stale recommendation from a current one.

The initial owner experience can be simple: choose the goal, confirm the business, add known constraints, and connect or provide evidence. Advanced fields can remain available in a details panel. Progressive disclosure should reduce unnecessary work without hiding uncertainty. If the owner does not know retention, the interface should explain what can still be decided and what requires a cautious scenario.

Implement arithmetic as a small domain library with defined units and missing-value behavior. For margin, reject an invalid target at or above 100% and avoid dividing by zero revenue. For payback, accumulate contribution over time and return an unrecovered result when appropriate. For capacity, compare equivalent time periods. For multicurrency analysis, require an explicit conversion policy and observation date. These are meaningful correctness requirements, not cosmetic checks.

A recommendation record should include its diagnosis, candidate alternatives, evidence references, assumptions, deterministic calculations, proposed actions, cost envelope, dependencies, review date, and invalidation triggers. A changed product price may invalidate acquisition economics without invalidating interview observations. A changed customer segment may require a much broader review. Use this dependency logic to refresh efficiently and preserve historical explanations.

Evaluate the module with realistic cases: profitable but cash-constrained commerce, high-signup low-retention software, a capacity-limited agency, a subscription product with expensive heavy users, and a business with almost no data. Include contradictory evidence and unknown costs. Passing means the system selects appropriate next decisions, labels uncertainty, performs correct arithmetic, and never fabricates business facts to complete a template. The module is useful when an owner can understand and challenge its reasoning, then act on a concrete, affordable experiment.

records.heading: Introduction
records.content:
# Book 02 — Customer Research and Positioning

*ClimbOS Growth Intelligence Library. Research cutoff: October 19, 2026. Frameworks and implementation policies proposed in this book are operating guidance, not measured industry benchmarks. All worked business examples are hypothetical unless explicitly identified as a sourced case.*

records.heading: 1. Research should change a decision
records.content:
Customer research earns its place when it changes what a business builds, promises, sells, or stops doing. A collection of attractive personas is not enough. Before collecting information, name the decision, the alternatives, the consequence of being wrong, and the observation that would change the decision. This turns research from an open-ended content exercise into an investment in reduced uncertainty.

Consider a small software business choosing between independent consultants and operations teams. Interviewing “people interested in productivity” cannot settle this choice. The decision requires information about recurring work, urgency, purchase authority, practical access to customers, and the cost of serving each segment. Write those uncertainties before recruiting. Otherwise the team will collect whichever stories are easiest to hear and call the resulting convenience sample a strategy.

Use a decision brief with five sentences. We need to decide whom to serve first. Our current preference is a stated segment for a stated reason. The most dangerous uncertainty is a specific unproven assumption. We will examine a defined set of observations. We will reconsider if an explicit contrary result appears. The brief should fit on one screen and remain attached to every resulting recommendation.

ClimbOS should begin its research workflow with this brief. A business owner can answer ordinary questions such as “Which customers are you considering?” and “What would be expensive to get wrong?” The system can translate those answers into research questions, but must preserve the owner's original wording. A generated research agenda becomes a proposal rather than an invisible change to the business goal.

records.heading: 2. Separate the customer, the user, and the buying situation
records.content:
A useful segment is a group of purchasing situations that can be served with sufficiently similar product capabilities, messaging, acquisition methods, and economics. Demographic similarity alone does not establish this. Two founders with the same company size may buy for different reasons: one needs a process working tomorrow; the other is replacing a system across several teams after a security review.

Identify the user who experiences the problem, the champion who advances the purchase, the payer who controls funds, the evaluator who checks suitability, and the approver who can stop adoption. One person can fill every role in a small business. In larger organizations the roles can conflict. A daily user may value speed while an approver values auditability. Positioning must acknowledge the buying system without trying to say everything to everyone at once.

Describe a segment using circumstances, frequency of the job, current alternative, buying trigger, consequences of failure, and access route. Add geography or company size when they alter the buying process or eligibility. “Small agencies onboarding several clients each month and manually chasing missing project information” is more operationally useful than “busy professionals aged thirty to forty-five.” It implies research questions, product requirements, and places to recruit participants.

The Jobs to Be Done lens concerns the progress people seek in particular circumstances and includes functional, social, and emotional dimensions. That conceptual foundation comes from the [Christensen Institute's explanation](https://www.christenseninstitute.org/theory/jobs-to-be-done/). The procedure developed here is an application of that lens: reconstruct the situation, identify the existing response, and examine what would make switching worthwhile. It is not a claim that one interview script can reveal every customer's motives.

records.heading: 3. Build an evidence ledger before a persona
records.content:
Research records should distinguish an observation from an interpretation. “The participant opened a spreadsheet and copied six rows” is an observation. “The participant needs automation” is an interpretation. “All agencies need automation” is an unjustified generalization. Keeping these levels separate makes disagreement useful: colleagues can inspect the same observation and offer competing explanations.

For every evidence item, store its origin, collection date, participant or account identifier, consent status where relevant, precise excerpt or event locator, and limitations. An anonymized identifier is usually sufficient for analysis. Store identifying information separately when possible. A published review can support the statement that one reviewer reported a problem; it cannot establish the prevalence of that problem among all customers.

Classify findings as measured, owner-reported, source-reported, assumption, inference, or calculated. These categories align with the ClimbOS engineering brief. A business owner's claim about customers is valuable input but should not silently become measured evidence. Likewise, a competitor's homepage establishes what that competitor publicly claims, rather than proving the claimed outcome occurred.

Create contradiction links. When one account says setup is easy and another abandons setup, the disagreement is information. Differences in task complexity, prior experience, permissions, or implementation support may explain it. Do not average contradictory statements into a bland conclusion. Preserve the conditional structure: setup appeared easy for experienced solo users and difficult for administrators importing historical records.

records.heading: 4. Choose methods according to uncertainty
records.content:
Use interviews to explore a buying story, observation to understand actual work, usability sessions to identify interaction barriers, surveys to estimate patterns within a known sampling frame, and commercial experiments to test behavior under an offer. None of these methods substitutes for all the others. A survey of newsletter subscribers may characterize subscribers while saying little about buyers who never join the newsletter.

When the uncertainty is whether a problem exists in practice, observe or reconstruct recent incidents. When the uncertainty is which words people understand, test comprehension. When the uncertainty is willingness to pay, seek a realistic commercial commitment with clear terms. When the uncertainty is implementation burden, run an assisted pilot and record every manual intervention. Match the method to the failure you are trying to avoid.

Start with the cheapest method that can provide decision-changing evidence. That may be reviewing existing support conversations before commissioning new interviews. However, support data overrepresents people who contacted support. Pair it with evidence from successful quiet customers and people who left. The point is not a ritual of “triangulation” but deliberate exposure to groups that the first dataset misses.

Set a stop rule before collecting. For exploratory interviews, a proposed rule might be to pause after two successive sessions fail to add a new decision-relevant buying barrier, while ensuring each chosen participant category is represented. This is a practical scheduling policy, not proof of statistical saturation. If the decision has high financial consequences or major subgroup differences, collect more evidence or explicitly narrow the conclusion.

records.heading: 5. Recruit for contrast rather than applause
records.content:
Recruit recent buyers, unsuccessful evaluators, people who chose an alternative, and customers who stopped using the product. Separate those categories in the analysis. A happy customer's explanation of a past purchase may be useful, but it does not reveal all the barriers faced by someone who never adopted. Recruiting only enthusiasts creates a particularly persuasive form of selection bias.

Use neutral invitations. State that the purpose is to understand how the person handled a particular task, that criticism is useful, and that the session is not a sales presentation. If compensation is offered, make it independent of positive feedback. Do not imply that participation guarantees access to unreleased capabilities. Any recording arrangement should be explicit before recording begins.

For a small business without a research panel, begin with authorized existing relationships, opt-in interview requests, relevant communities that permit research recruitment, and introductions. ClimbOS must not pretend it owns a prospect database. It can help write recruitment materials and organize owner-supplied contacts, but sending messages requires the appropriate recipient, channel, and authorization checks. A generated list of plausible people is not a verified contact list.

Use a recruitment matrix rather than a rigid quota presented as science. For example, aim initially to hear from several recent buyers, several nonbuyers, and several former users, then adjust based on contradictions. Record who was invited, who accepted, who declined, and why when voluntarily disclosed. Nonresponse does not reveal a motive, but knowing its extent prevents the team from describing respondents as the entire market.

records.heading: 6. Conduct interviews around an actual episode
records.content:
Begin with a recent concrete event: “Tell me about the last time you prepared a client handoff.” Ask what happened first, what triggered the task, who became involved, which tools appeared, what went wrong, and what the person did next. Follow the sequence before asking for general opinions. The sequence often reveals constraints that disappear in a polished explanation of how work is supposed to happen.

Ask for artifacts when participants can share them appropriately: a blank template, a redacted checklist, or a demonstration with fictional data. Never require private client information simply to make an interview vivid. Observe transitions between tools. A complaint about “too many spreadsheets” might actually be a complaint about uncertain responsibility, duplicate entry, or waiting for approvals. Each implies a different solution.

Separate past behavior from future intention. “I would definitely use this” is weaker commercial evidence than “we paid an employee to solve this last week,” although neither guarantees a future purchase. Ask about the last expenditure, the approval conversation, and the alternative considered. Avoid defending the product when the participant misunderstands it; misunderstanding is itself useful evidence for positioning.

End by asking what would make switching unacceptable, who else should be consulted, and what important question was missed. Then summarize the story back in neutral language. Let the participant correct it. Keep any product demonstration until after the discovery portion, and mark statements collected after exposure to the demonstration so they are not mistaken for unprompted needs.

records.heading: 7. Turn interview material into decision evidence
records.content:
Analyze interviews in two passes. First extract concrete facts, quotations, events, and reported constraints without forcing them into a preferred framework. Then interpret patterns across cases. This order reduces the temptation to make every participant confirm the category the team hoped to find. A short, accurate event summary is often more useful than pages of sentiment labels.

Create a codebook with definitions and counterexamples. “Urgency” might require a specific deadline or visible consequence of delay; enthusiastic adjectives alone do not qualify. “Switching barrier” might include data migration, stakeholder approval, lost integrations, or fear of interruption. If multiple analysts apply the same code differently, revise the definition and revisit a sample rather than concealing inconsistency behind a combined chart.

Count participants and accounts separately. Five interviews from one company do not provide five independent company buying decisions. Preserve denominators when describing findings: “four of seven interviewed accounts reported manual reconciliation” is inspectable. “Most companies struggle with reconciliation” is broader than the evidence. Qualitative counts help organize a sample; they do not automatically estimate market prevalence.

Maintain negative cases. If the proposed segment values a workflow but one participant rejects it, explain why. Perhaps the person's existing system is sufficient or the pain occurs too rarely. These exceptions can define eligibility better than another enthusiastic endorsement. A precise exclusion can save more acquisition money than a broad promise attracts.

records.heading: 8. Assess problem importance without false precision
records.content:
Use an importance profile rather than one magic score. Examine frequency, consequence, current effort, budget relevance, urgency, and access to authority. Score each on a small, documented scale only to support comparison. A score should summarize evidence, never replace it. Unknown values should remain unknown rather than becoming a convenient midpoint.

One proposed comparison formula is `priority = severity × recurrence × readiness × confidence / delivery_effort`. Each factor must use a stated scale and the same definitions across candidates. This formula is a prioritization heuristic, not a statistical model. Multiplication makes weak readiness consequential: a severe problem with no route to purchase may be a poor immediate target despite long-term importance.

For a hypothetical agency task, severity is four out of five, recurrence four, readiness three, confidence 0.6, and delivery effort three. The resulting index is 9.6. Another segment scores severity five, recurrence two, readiness one, confidence 0.4, and effort four, producing 1.0. The difference suggests where to investigate first; it does not predict nine times more revenue.

Supplement the index with a written reason against the choice. Perhaps the attractive segment requires a missing integration or unusually intensive support. If one prerequisite makes the offer impossible, use an eligibility gate before scoring. A business that cannot legally or technically serve a segment should not let an impressive numerical ranking override that constraint.

records.heading: 9. Map alternatives customers actually use
records.content:
The competitive set includes specialist tools, general tools, internal processes, outsourced services, and doing nothing. Ask which alternative was used in the last real episode. A customer who handles a task through email is not necessarily evaluating a category of software. Their comparison may be between tolerated inconvenience and a new administrative responsibility.

Build an alternatives matrix with the job, current method, reason chosen, frustration, switching cost, and evidence source. Add public competitor facts only after checking their own current documentation. Record dates because prices and feature availability change. Avoid declaring a competitor deficient because a page did not mention a capability. Absence from one retrieved page is not proof of absence from the product.

Distinguish parity requirements from differentiators. A capability may be essential for eligibility yet provide little reason to switch because every viable alternative has it. Conversely, a distinctive feature is commercially irrelevant if the target segment does not value it. Positioning requires a meaningful difference in the chosen comparison frame, not simply a longer feature list.

Use a “why stay?” analysis alongside “why buy?” The existing method may be familiar, approved, already paid for, and integrated into habits. A replacement must overcome that accumulated convenience. Sometimes the right offer is an add-on that reduces one painful step, rather than an ambitious all-in-one replacement. Research should leave that strategic option open.

records.heading: 10. Construct a defensible position
records.content:
A position connects a specific customer situation to a valuable outcome through a credible mechanism, relative to the alternatives that customer considers. Write it internally as: for a defined segment facing a defined circumstance, our offer helps achieve a defined outcome through a stated mechanism; compared with the current alternative, the relevant difference is a verifiable distinction.

The internal statement is not necessarily homepage copy. It is a reasoning tool. Every clause should have either evidence or a hypothesis label. If the mechanism is still proposed, do not publish it as an existing feature. If the outcome depends on customer effort, say so when constructing the offer. A claim that omits a decisive condition can be persuasive and misleading at the same time.

Strategyzer's [Value Proposition Canvas](https://www.strategyzer.com/library/the-value-proposition-canvas) separates a customer profile of jobs, pains, and gains from the offer that addresses them. Use that established framework as a diagnostic: identify important needs and explain how the offer meets them. The additional position contract here adds evidence links, alternative comparisons, and claim approval to make the reasoning executable inside ClimbOS.

Choose a category customers can recognize unless there is strong evidence that an unfamiliar category improves comprehension. A novel category can create explanation costs. When the product spans categories, lead with the buying situation rather than listing every function. A position is a choice about which value to make easiest to understand first.

records.heading: 11. Translate the position into a message hierarchy
records.content:
Build messages in layers. The first layer states the situation and outcome. The second explains the mechanism. The third offers proof and answers the main objection. The final layer supplies detailed capabilities and operational conditions. This structure lets a hurried visitor understand relevance while allowing a serious evaluator to inspect support.

For a hypothetical client-intake tool, an initial message might be “Start projects with the information your team needs.” A supporting sentence could describe a verified collection and review workflow if one exists. If no such capability has been verified, the sentence stays in a concept-testing document. Do not transfer illustrative copy into a real business campaign without checking actual product facts.

Create a claims register. Each claim needs exact wording, support, scope, expiration or review date, and approval status. “Save hours every week” requires evidence about hours, tasks, users, and the observation period. Without such evidence, communicate the mechanism or intended benefit in bounded terms. Evidence should improve the promise, not appear as a footnote attached to an otherwise unsupported headline.

Different buying roles may need different supporting proof while sharing one core position. The daily user needs to see the task completed. The payer needs a plausible economic case. The approver needs appropriate controls. Create role-specific sections or assets instead of forcing every concern into a single overloaded hero paragraph.

records.heading: 12. Test comprehension before persuasion
records.content:
A message test should first ask whether the reader understands the offer. Show a page or short statement, remove it, and ask what the product does, who it is for, and what the next action would achieve. Do not explain missing meaning during the test. Confusion at this stage makes click-through comparisons difficult to interpret because different readers may be responding to different imagined products.

Then test relevance and credibility. Ask which situation the message reminds the participant of, what seems useful, what sounds doubtful, and what would need verification before proceeding. These questions identify both attraction and friction. Asking only “Which headline do you like?” produces a preference contest that may reward novelty rather than commercial clarity.

Use behavioral tests when the offer is sufficiently real. A small landing-page experiment can compare qualified inquiries, completed onboarding, or another meaningful action. Keep traffic source, eligibility, and follow-up comparable. Clicks alone can select a provocative message that attracts the wrong audience. Define the downstream quality measure before running the test.

Do not announce a winner from a handful of conversions. With small samples, report counts, uncertainty, and alternative explanations. A practical decision may still be necessary, but it should be framed as provisional. ClimbOS can recommend the clearer option while stating that commercial superiority remains unproven and scheduling a review after a defined evidence window.

records.heading: 13. Work a complete hypothetical example
records.content:
Imagine a fictional software company considering an intake product for independent consultants and small agencies. This is not a statement about Formkit's actual capabilities or market. The owner has ten research conversations: four consultants, four agencies, and two former users of another tool. The sample was recruited through existing relationships and therefore cannot estimate either market's prevalence.

The consultant stories emphasize occasional confusion and a desire to look professional. Agency stories emphasize repeated handoffs between sales and delivery. Three agencies show recent redacted checklists; two describe project delays after missing information. One agency is satisfied with its existing system and would not migrate. The strongest pattern is not “everyone wants better forms,” but a specific handoff problem under repeated delivery pressure.

The initial choice is to investigate agencies that onboard several projects and have separate sales and delivery responsibilities. The evidence against this choice is implementation complexity: two agencies require integrations the fictional product lacks. The position therefore narrows further to teams whose current approved workflow can accept a lightweight additional collection step. This exclusion makes the pilot feasible.

The pilot offer proposes one onboarding workflow, assisted setup, and a review after three completed handoffs. Hypothetical evaluation criteria are less missing information at delivery, time spent chasing inputs, and whether the delivery lead chooses to continue. No claim of revenue improvement is made. If setup consumes more staff time than it saves during the observed period, the team revisits the workflow or target rather than celebrating signups.

records.heading: 14. Estimate economic value carefully
records.content:
A simple time-value model is `monthly_capacity_value = eligible_events × minutes_saved_per_event / 60 × loaded_hourly_cost`. Use compatible units and identify every input as measured or assumed. This calculation estimates released capacity under its assumptions. It does not automatically equal cash savings, profit, or incremental revenue. A salaried employee saving time may simply have more capacity for other work.

Suppose, hypothetically, a team handles twenty eligible handoffs monthly, saves twelve minutes each, and values staff capacity at thirty dollars per hour. The calculation gives one hundred twenty dollars of monthly capacity value. If setup requires four hours, include that cost and the period over which it is assessed. The product's subscription is only one part of the switching decision.

For avoided errors, use `expected_avoided_cost = event_volume × change_in_error_probability × average_consequence_cost`. The change in probability needs credible evidence. With no baseline, present low, middle, and high assumptions instead of a single confident value. Avoid double-counting time spent fixing errors if that time is already included in the time-saving estimate.

Ask what would make the benefit realizable. Saving time in a task that is not a bottleneck may have little effect on throughput. An attractive theoretical return can fail because the buyer lacks implementation capacity. Use the model to identify sensitive assumptions and ask better questions, rather than presenting a precise-looking return as a guaranteed outcome.

records.heading: 15. Use AI to accelerate analysis without fabricating customers
records.content:
AI can propose interview questions, summarize authorized transcripts, suggest codes, identify contradictions, and draft candidate positions. Each output should remain linked to original evidence. The highest-value automation is often organizing messy material so a human can inspect it quickly. Automated confidence phrasing cannot substitute for traceable observations.

Treat a generated persona as a hypothesis document. It is not a research participant. Simulated answers can help rehearse a script or reveal assumptions in a concept, but they must not enter a customer-evidence denominator. Keep synthetic material in a separate namespace and display its status prominently. A plausible quotation invented by a model is still invented.

Create an extraction task that requests episode, trigger, alternative, constraint, quote locator, and uncertainty. Require `null` when the transcript does not answer a field. Follow with deterministic checks that the cited locator exists and that the output did not introduce a capability absent from the business snapshot. A second review can inspect a sample for fidelity before scaled processing.

OpenAI's [Structured Outputs announcement](https://openai.com/index/introducing-structured-outputs-in-the-api/) describes schema-constrained output. In this workflow, that capability can help produce consistent records. Schema validity does not establish factual accuracy. ClimbOS still needs evidence resolution, contradiction handling, authorization boundaries, and evaluation of extraction errors. Model choice should follow the existing OpenAI-first engine and repository evidence rather than a new provider assumption.

records.heading: 16. Research playbook: episode discovery
records.content:
The following is an illustrative configuration contract. Identifiers name fixture evidence, not real customers. Thresholds are proposed operational policies that should be changed when the decision or risk changes.

```yaml
playbook_id: customer_episode_discovery_v1
status: proposed
objective: choose_a_feasible_initial_segment
inputs:
  business_snapshot_id: fixture_snapshot_01
  decision_id: fixture_segment_decision_01
  authorized_dataset_ids: []
  evidence_required: true
recruitment:
  categories:
    - recent_buyer
    - evaluated_without_buying
    - former_user
  contact_database_available: false
  sending_authorization_required: true
interview:
  start_with: most_recent_relevant_episode
  extract:
    - trigger
    - sequence
    - existing_alternative
    - buying_roles
    - switching_barriers
    - concrete_consequences
  prohibited:
    - invented_quotes
    - synthetic_participants_as_evidence
analysis:
  unit_of_comparison: account_buying_situation
  retain_negative_cases: true
  unknown_value: null
output:
  evidence_ledger: required
  candidate_segments: required
  contradictions: required
  decision_recommendation: provisional
execution:
  publish: false
  send_messages: false
  spend_money: false
```

To implement this playbook, validate the snapshot and authorized datasets first. Create recruitment tasks only for sources actually available. Store each transcript or note under an account-scoped research record. Run extraction, then present a review screen with the extracted claim beside its source passage. A reviewer can accept, revise, reject, or mark it unresolved.

The decision output should include the recommended segment, the strongest evidence for it, the strongest evidence against it, and the next observation that could reverse the recommendation. If the evidence does not distinguish candidates, say so. A useful research engine can return “not yet distinguishable” and prescribe a narrower experiment instead of manufacturing a winner.

records.heading: 17. Position evaluation playbook
records.content:
```json
{
  "playbook_id": "position_evaluation_v1",
  "status": "proposed",
  "position": {
    "segment_id": "fixture_segment_agency_handoffs",
    "situation": "Repeated sales-to-delivery handoffs",
    "desired_outcome": "A complete information handoff",
    "mechanism_claim_id": null,
    "alternative_ids": ["fixture_manual_checklist"]
  },
  "gates": [
    {"id": "product_truth", "pass_requires": "All capability claims resolve to approved evidence"},
    {"id": "eligibility", "pass_requires": "Segment can use the actual offer"},
    {"id": "comprehension", "pass_requires": "Reviewers can state task and intended user without coaching"}
  ],
  "comparison_criteria": ["relevance", "credibility", "difference", "commercial_feasibility"],
  "unknown_policy": "Do not replace missing evidence with a score",
  "output": {
    "decision": "provisional",
    "approved_for_publication": false,
    "required_evidence_ids": [],
    "reasons_against": [],
    "next_test": "Observed completion of a real eligible workflow"
  }
}
```

This contract makes publication a distinct state. A position can be analytically promising while its public claims remain unapproved. That separation matters because strategy generation is not authorization to publish or send. A future execution service should accept approved exact claim versions, not a vague assurance that a strategy document was reviewed sometime earlier.

The evaluation should also compare a candidate against the current position. Repositioning has costs: existing customers may be confused, supporting pages may conflict, and sales materials may need revision. Require a migration inventory before changing the public story. The purpose of testing is to improve commercial understanding, not to generate perpetual headline churn.

records.heading: 18. A decision tree for research and positioning
records.content:
If business identity or product facts are uncertain, verify the canonical domain and current offer before proposing a position. If identity is known but the customer problem is vague, reconstruct recent episodes. If the problem is concrete but purchasing behavior differs across accounts, segment by circumstance and buying process. If the segment is clear but the mechanism is unverified, run a capability or workflow check.

If the mechanism is credible but people misunderstand it, test simpler category language and message order. If people understand the promise but do not care, reconsider relevance or urgency before changing button colors. If people care but will not switch, investigate implementation cost, risk, authority, and the existing alternative. If people try and leave, examine delivered value rather than assuming the acquisition message needs more intensity.

When evidence conflicts, first ask whether the records concern the same job, customer type, period, and product version. If they do not, retain separate conditional conclusions. If they do, collect a discriminating observation. Do not solve disagreement by counting more weak opinions against fewer strong behavioral records without considering what each record can actually establish.

Stop research when the remaining uncertainty is unlikely to change the next affordable decision. Continue when the uncertainty could cause a consequential irreversible choice. This is a judgment about decision exposure and information value, not a universal number of interviews. Keep the stopping rationale visible in the research record.

records.heading: 19. Implement the knowledge inside ClimbOS
records.content:
Add proposed domain entities for research decisions, participants, evidence items, episode summaries, segment hypotheses, position versions, claim approvals, and evaluation runs. Reuse existing schema and authorization conventions after repository inspection. Convex should hold tenant-scoped state and workflow progress; the Vercel application should expose review, comparison, and approval surfaces. These are recommendations, not claims about functionality already shipped.

Store evidence separately from interpretations so one source can support several hypotheses without being duplicated. An interpretation should reference source identifiers and the exact snapshot used. A new product price, capability change, or contradictory customer record should invalidate affected claims for review. Historical positions must remain explainable even after the current recommendation changes.

The default owner interface should show three things: who the current recommendation serves, why that choice is plausible, and what remains uncertain. Advanced views can expose sampling, coding, score assumptions, and calculations. Use ordinary language in the main view; do not require a nontechnical owner to understand an embedding index before approving a research conclusion.

Resend can be considered for authorized research invitations and follow-up messages where supported by actual implementation and sending policies. It should not become an assumed cold-outreach engine. Keep suppression and contact permissions separate from analytical interest. A person being an attractive interview candidate does not establish that their address is available or that an invitation is authorized.

records.heading: 20. Evaluate research quality and maintain the system
records.content:
Build a frozen evaluation set containing clear episodes, ambiguous episodes, contradictory records, missing fields, synthetic fixtures, and adversarial source text. Check whether the system extracts only supported details, preserves uncertainty, identifies buying roles correctly, and keeps synthetic examples out of evidence. Include examples where the correct recommendation is to defer judgment.

Measure decision usefulness with human review. Can an owner understand the segment? Can a reviewer inspect the supporting evidence? Does the next experiment discriminate between competing explanations? Track unsupported claim rate and evidence-locator accuracy alongside cost and latency. A long report or a large number of citations is not sufficient evidence of quality.

Review research when a major product capability changes, a segment repeatedly fails onboarding, a new alternative changes buying criteria, or current evidence becomes stale. Do not refresh everything on a fixed schedule without considering materiality. Stable conceptual frameworks may remain useful while competitor prices or platform permissions need immediate verification.

The completed operating loop is decision, evidence, interpretation, position, test, and revision. Its commercial value comes from disciplined choices. ClimbOS should help owners make those choices with less effort while preserving the difference between a compelling story and a supported conclusion.

records.heading: 21. Run a two-week positioning sprint
records.content:
A short research sprint needs a bounded question and protected analysis time. On the first day, write the decision brief, inventory existing evidence, and identify the most consequential gaps. On the second day, prepare recruitment and a neutral episode script. Keep the first sessions exploratory. If every question assumes the product is the answer, rewrite the script before recruiting more people.

During the middle of the sprint, alternate collection with analysis. After each session, capture an episode summary, one surprising observation, one contradiction, and one implication that remains tentative. This small discipline prevents a final-day synthesis from relying on whichever interview was most memorable. Revise recruitment if an important buying role or a contrasting case is absent, but record the change so the final sample can be understood.

At the end of the first week, create two candidate positions and an explicit status-quo alternative. Describe what each would require the company to be good at. One may demand fast self-service setup; another may require expert implementation support. Positioning is partly an operating commitment. A message that attracts customers the business cannot serve is a weak strategy even when the words test well.

In the second week, test comprehension, check capability claims, and run the smallest feasible workflow demonstration. Review the alternatives using the same criteria. Document why the preferred position wins provisionally, what evidence is still missing, and which customer situations should be excluded from the initial offer. Finish with an implementation backlog covering product gaps, page changes, sales explanations, measurement, and the next commercial test.

The final sprint artifact should remain compact enough to use. A position statement, evidence map, objections list, claims register, and experiment card are sufficient when each links to deeper records. Avoid turning a useful research result into a large presentation nobody consults. In ClimbOS, these artifacts should be connected views over the same versioned data rather than separately generated documents that can contradict one another.

A sprint fails constructively when it shows that the original choice cannot yet be made. For example, available interviews may describe users while omitting buyers, or the preferred promise may depend on an unbuilt capability. Mark those gaps as blockers and propose the next focused observation. Do not reward the system for generating a polished position regardless of evidence. Reward it for reducing the risk of a bad commercial commitment.
